'''John Marzluff''' (born 1958) is a professor of wildlife science at the [[University of Washington]] and an author.

''In the Company of Crows and Ravens'' was written with and illustrated by Tony Angell.<ref name=MarzluffCA/> They discuss the ways that crows are like humans, and the many different ways that humans have treated crows.<ref name=MarzluffCA>[https://www.encyclopedia.com/arts/educational-magazines/marzluff-john-m "Marzluff, John M."]. Contemporary Authors, Encyclopedia.com. Retrieved July 30, 2020.</ref> In ''Gifts of the Crow'', Marzluff and Angell documented how intelligent crows are, with both anecdotes and research.<ref>Gorman, James. [https://www.nytimes.com/2012/06/12/science/gifts-of-the-crow-and-bird-sense-the-lives-of-the-winged-set.html "The Games Crows Play, and Other Winged Tales"] New York Times, June 11, 2012. Retrieved June 30, 2020.</ref> In ''Subirdia'', Marzluff shows how seven "exploiter" birds have enlarged their territories by taking advantage of human-made changes to the environment, and discusses how we could make our back yards better for birds.<ref name=Bodio>Bodio, Stephen, J. [https://www.allaboutbirds.org/news/book-review-welcome-to-subirdia-by-john-marzluff/ "Book Review: Welcome To Subirdia, By John Marzluff"]. allaboutbirds.org April 14, 2015. Retrieved June 30, 2020.</ref> His work combines science, anecdotes, and humor.<ref name=Bodio/>

His lab once banded American crows while wearing various masks, which demonstrated that crows identify and remember people's faces.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2008/08/26/science/26crow.html|title=Friend or Foe? Crows Never Forget a Face, It Seems|date=26 August 2008|work=The New York Times}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=American crows: the ultimate angry birds? |url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/punctuated-equilibrium/2011/jul/06/2 |work=GrrlScientist |publisher=The Guardian |date=July 2, 2011}}</ref> After the people wearing the mask left, even crows that did not witness the tagging scolded the mask, showing an example of cultural transmission in crows. He and his fellow researchers found that this transmission was both from one generation to the next and from peer to peer.<ref name=Marzluff2011>Cornell, H; Marzluff, J; Pecoraro, S. [https://royalsocietypublishing.org/doi/10.1098/rspb.2011.0957 Social learning spreads knowledge about dangerous humans among American crows]. Proceedings of the Royal Society. 2011. Retrieved July 30, 2020.</ref> His work is featured on the PBS documentary TV show [[Nature (TV series)|''Nature'']] in the episode "A Murder of Crows".<ref>{{cite web|url=http://video.pbs.org/video/1621910826/|title=Watch Full Episodes Online of Nature on PBS - A Murder of Crows|work=PBS}}{{dead link|date=June 2025|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}}</ref> His work with crows includes some of the first behavioral brain-imaging studies in wild birds.<ref name=McGowan>McGowan, Kat. [https://www.audubon.org/magazine/march-april-2016/meet-bird-brainiacs-american-crow "Meet the Bird Brainiacs"]. ''Audubon'', March–April 2016. Retrieved July 30, 2020.</ref>

In 1989, he won the H.R. Painton Award for an outstanding paper published in ''The Condor''.<ref name=MarzluffCA/>
